newsitem.title: USA: Houston tax vote seen as a "squeaker".
newsitem.headline: Houston tax vote seen as a "squeaker".

text.p: Political experts said they expected a "squeaker" on Saturday when the city of Houston votes on a proposition that would limit City Hall's ability to raise taxes.

Polls early on showed that so-called Proposition A would pass easily, but a late campaign against the initiative, led by Mayor Bob Lanier, had closed the gap and made the election a toss-up, they said.

"Proposition A had been likely to pass by a 2-1 margin, but that has narrowed considerably...what I saw (of polling results) was too close to call," said Rice University political scientist Bob Stein.
"There's a good groundswell of business opposition, but it's going to be a squeaker," he told Reuters.
A very low turnout -- perhaps 100,000 voters -- was expected and cold, icy weather has been forecast for Saturday. Those two factors added to the uncertainty of the outcome, experts said.

Proposition A, put forth by an anti-tax group called Tax Vote '97, would require citywide elections on proposed increases in taxes and fees. It follows recent tax-limiting measures passed in California and Oregon.

The point, said proponents, is to limit city spending, which they believe has spiraled out of sight. "There is a time to say no. That's what Proposition A is all about," said Tax Vote '97 organizer Bruce Hotze.
But opponents argue that the initiative would result in an endless string of elections, put a stranglehold on City Hall, and, in the end, cost more money than it would save.

"This is the worst drafted piece of legislation I've seen in my entire life. It will not limit your taxes, it will cost you money -- I estimate $100 million over the next 12 years," Lanier told a business group this week.
The $100 million in increased costs would be the result of lower bond ratings if Proposition A passes, Lanier said.

Rating agencies Standard & Poor's and Moody's have already said the passage of Proposition A could have negative implications for the city's bond ratings because of its possible effect on the ability to govern.

City Controller Lloyd Kelley told the city council on Wednesday that fears about the election boosted interest rates in a bond sale last week and kept one regular customer, an insurance company, from even entering the bidding. He estimated the extra interest costs for the sale at $1.5 million.
But Hotze, speaking to the same business group as Lanier, said it was unlikely that Proposition A would lower bond ratings and accused the mayor of using scare tactics to influence the vote.
"The mayor's analysis must have come from the law firm of Dewey Taxem and How," he said.

Lanier, in an indication of the bitter feelings the election has generated, shot back: "It appears to me that this mess (Proposition A) was drawn up by Curly, Larry and Moe," referring to the comedy team The Three Stooges.

Stein said the well-financed forces against the initiative were lining up a strong turnout among minority voters, who were more likely to oppose the measure than white voters. In a recent election on whether to build a new baseball stadium, a similar effort to get out minority voters helped overcome anti-tax opposition to narrowly approve the stadium.
Also, on the ballot on Saturday will be a proposal to raise the city's minimum wage to $6.50 an hour, well above the current federal minimum wage of $4.75.

The minimum wage proposal was the brainchild of organized labor and other grassroots groups, but has come under heavy fire from business groups who say it will result in the city losing 52,000 jobs. It was expected to lose by large margin, Stein said.
